title: The Jamharah Ode of Adi ibn Zayd
intro: Ibn Sallam singles out this opening among Adi ibn Zayd's verses, and Abu Zayd al-Qurashi includes the ode among the poems called the Mujamharat. Adi stops at Umm Ma'bad's abandoned home, where longing leaves him unsteady and a woman's reproaches call for an answer. A private exchange grows into advice about the company one keeps and the claims friends have on one another. It ends with the sound of voices mourning the speaker himself.

translation: Do you recognise what remains of Umm Ma'bad's home?
Yes. Longing strikes you after all your show of strength.
1.sharh: Recognition is instantaneous. The force of longing comes as a blow after the effort it took to hold himself together.

translation: I stayed there all day, drinking longing, as though
my drinking companions had poured me a generous draught.
2.sharh: Longing goes in like a drink. The deserted site can leave him as unsteady as a full measure poured in company.

translation: What longing that was, what a visitation of tears,
soaking my shirtfront with no one to weep beside me.
3.sharh: Tears run down to the opening at his neck. The wet cloth is tangible evidence of grief that no companion has stayed to witness.

translation: A woman rose in the night to blame me.
When she went too far, I told her, “Keep some measure.”
4.sharh: Night gives the rebuke a human voice. His first answer asks her to limit how far she goes.

translation: Woman, blame misplaced and aimed at me
only doubles your recurring error.
5.sharh: A rebuke that misses its object can be repeated without growing any truer. His turn of phrase makes the repetition itself part of her mistake.

translation: Critic, you have spoken long and missed the mark.
If you are astray, set yourself straight.
6.sharh: She has assumed the right to direct him. He returns the task to her with her own conduct as its first object.

translation: Critic, folly is part of a man's abasement.
Death lies in wait for men.
7.sharh: Folly lowers a person's standing, and time to do better is short. The Jamhara gives “pleasure” where the recitation and diwan have “abasement.”

translation: Critic, how close sound judgement lies to a man,
how far from him if he lacks guidance.
8.sharh: The right course can be within reach and still go untaken. Near and far describe a person's ability to find it.

translation: Critic, whoever is allotted the Fire meets it
face to face. Whoever is allotted deliverance prospers.
9.sharh: The repetition of “allotted” holds the alternatives together. Whichever fate is written, meeting it will be personal and direct.

translation: Critic, I have met what can restrain a man.
In two anklets I matched a prisoner's steps.
10.sharh: The rings at the ankles dictate the length of a step. Al-Mu'aybid's note hears a comparison with the uncertain gait of a drinker in this image of confinement.

translation: Critic, what can you know beyond a guess
about an hour today or the morning of tomorrow?
11.sharh: The question withholds what the hour will bring. A parallel version names his death outright, making the limits of what she can know particularly stark.

translation: Leave me. What good is ruin already gone by?
What should I want of it, as my visitors grow few?
12.sharh: He turns from the prospect of ruin to the sickbed with its dwindling visitors. Another transmission makes the thought about property explicit, asking what wealth a dying man has sent ahead of him.

translation: My death has been appointed its time.
I shall be left, laid on a pillow or without one.
13.sharh: The appointed hour reduces a great question to the smallest kindness. Whether someone is there to cushion his head cannot change the outcome.

translation: The wealth that remains goes to my heir. Give up
reproaching me. I am putting things right, doing no harm.
14.sharh: The heir will have whatever is left. His defence of spending rests on what he can do with wealth while the decision is still his.

translation: Critic, whoever fails to put himself right alone,
away from the tribe, gains little guidance from a faultfinder.
15.sharh: The measure of character is what happens beyond the camp's sight. Another person's rebukes have little purchase where self-correction never begins.

translation: A man's own days are warning enough.
They bring him lessons at evening and at dawn.
16.sharh: Morning and evening make two visits every day. Experience has more opportunities to admonish him than the woman speaking to him now.

translation: I have been tried, and I have put men to the test.
Long years now stand between me and my birth.
17.sharh: The same root gives him both roles, the tested man and the tester of others. The years intervening since his birth lend weight to his reply.

translation: I am no first among men for whom events
have brought good fortune in the wake of hardship.
18.sharh: The densely packed nouns make the construction difficult. Its thread is the familiar reversal of men's fortunes, hardship giving way to happier times.

translation: Guard yourself from going astray and speaking foully.
Mislead yourself, and the man following you goes astray.
19.sharh: The reach of a private failing now extends to anyone watching for an example. The echoed verb follows the error from one person to another.

translation: If you owe someone a kindness,
return its like to the claimant and add something more.
20.sharh: He treats a kindness received as a claim on its recipient. Matching it discharges the claim, while a little more keeps generosity in circulation.

translation: If your friendship does its people no good,
and hardship from you leaves your enemy unscathed, away with you.
21.sharh: He measures a declaration of loyalty by its consequences. The brusque dismissal falls on someone whose friends and enemies experience him in much the same way.

translation: If a man can look for no leniency from you,
expect none from him, nor protection in a dangerous hour.
22.sharh: Someone who has learned to expect no concession will remember it when their places are reversed. The second test comes in a situation where one person needs another's protection.

translation: When you banter with men, do not take offence.
Answer in their own vein and keep your temper.
23.sharh: A person who joins the teasing must leave room for a reply. The danger comes when he finds he can make a joke more readily than he can take one.

translation: When you ask others for a gift,
show restraint. Press too hard and you will go wanting.
24.sharh: The advice allows for real need. Pressing a request too insistently risks losing both the gift and the dignity of asking for it.

translation: Beware of too much joking. It can
make a fool even of a steady, judicious man.
25.sharh: The warning includes a man already known for good judgement. A reputation for joking can make even his serious words easy to discount.

translation: You will get all you are due from a foul-mouthed man
by taking him gently, without yet needing firmness.
26.sharh: Forbearance need not cost the claimant a thing. He may receive the whole of what he is owed before there is any need to press harder.

translation: Many a man manages what his father never managed,
reaching after the means to do what he never learned.
27.sharh: He turns to people undertaking unfamiliar work. A father's experience sets no final limit on what the next man may try.

translation: One inherits distinction he never attained himself.
Another wins fresh honour of his own, newly earned.
28.sharh: His words for newly gained and inherited honour are also words for property. The heir and the founder can possess standing by quite different routes.

translation: Another hopes for many things he'll never reach.
Death will part him from them for the grave.
29.sharh: He calls death by a name that carries the idea of separating. The neighbouring verb echoes it as the hopeful man is parted from his projects.

translation: Keep up the labour behind what you have inherited.
Add all the good you can earn for yourself.
30.sharh: An inheritance carries work with it. Preserving it gives the heir a starting point from which to add something attributable to him.

translation: Turn your words elsewhere, and remember
that today's first sign of distance means a breach tomorrow.
31.sharh: The clue is a small coolness already perceptible today. In the reading explained by Ibn Qutayba it warns of a friend who may break with you tomorrow.

translation: Ask about a man's companion instead of the man.
Every companion takes his fellow as an example.
32.sharh: He makes the companion evidence of character. The repeated sounds of the words for keeping company enact the likeness that grows between the two.

translation: If the man is given to evil, leave his side at once.
If he is good, keep his company and find your way.
33.sharh: The preceding observation becomes a decision about where to stand. Good company can teach simply by remaining close at hand.

translation: A wrong done by one's own kin cuts deeper
than the stroke of a keen Indian sword.
34.sharh: A man looks to his family for protection, which gives a kinsman's wrong its second sting. The Jamhara preserves the verse under both poets. In Tarafa's ode the blow falls “on a man”, the wording heard here. In Adi's it falls “on the soul”.

translation: When you see mischief rouse its people
and the makers of trouble stand up for it, stay seated.
35.sharh: Wrongdoing recruits a crowd before any one individual has acted. The answer he prescribes is a bodily decision, keeping one's seat when the others rise.

translation: When you are among people, befriend their best.
Keep the worst company and you'll come to grief with them.
36.sharh: The Arabic words for the worst man and for coming to grief sound close. It is as though his companion's downfall is already audible in his name.

translation: Speak justly when you speak, and spare needless blame.
Blame where blame is due and praise the praiseworthy.
37.sharh: Having warned against blame as a habit, he gives praise and criticism their proper objects. Fair speech requires the speaker to distinguish between cases.

translation: Reproach only someone who has earned it. Spare your blame.
Meet your friend's complaint with an open hand.
38.sharh: The friend who complains may need something more practical than a judgement. In the parallel reading generosity buys the giver's release from the complaint.

translation: Someone who comes to you in need, whom you deny
what he asks today, may grieve you tomorrow.
39.sharh: Today's applicant may be in a position to cause hurt tomorrow. A parallel tradition imagines the same reversal as the applicant's new prosperity.

translation: People have humiliation in store for a miser
who hoards. The stingy are abased and held cheap.
40.sharh: What the miser retains in goods is set against a loss of standing. Others can answer his refusal by lowering the value they set on him.

translation: For one bent on refusing, the first refusal
is the more decent. A miser earns blame and rough handling.
41.sharh: For someone set on refusing, a prompt refusal at least spares the applicant a false hope. The verse still leaves the habitual miser open to blame and ill treatment.

translation: The days and the passage of time disclosed this to me.
I set it down. Whoever fails to put things right spoils them.
42.sharh: “I set it down” interrupts the maxim like the writer's signature. Experience has taught him that neglect alone can spoil what is in someone's care.

translation: I have tasted a young man's pleasures. I have been struck
by blows whose survivor might live for ever.
43.sharh: He has known pleasure at first hand, which gives its opposite equal weight. The promise of endless life measures the ordeal in deliberately extravagant terms.

translation: When you detest a trait in someone,
shun it yourself and strike elsewhere with the mourner's cloth.
44.sharh: The advice begins with the difference between judging a trait and practising it. The striking-cloth image that follows is obscure. A parallel version tells the listener to aim for a different course.

translation: The man with no defender when his claim is at stake
is overborne by the one with backing and is oppressed.
45.sharh: The person with the better claim can lose to the one with supporters. It is the unequal ability to enforce a claim that concerns him.

translation: Many hands can hold oppression in check
when men's hands are present where a claim is heard.
46.sharh: The gathering supplies the missing support of the previous verse. The repetition of “hands” suggests witnesses ready to act.

translation: An undertaking that admits of ease ends better
than a difficult affair passed back and forth.
47.sharh: His test is the final outcome. A difficult business can pass from hand to hand until nothing is accomplished.

translation: I shall win renown, or my own last hour will come
upon me by night, my mourners and my visitors there.
48.sharh: The vow allows him the rest of his life for the pursuit of honour. Mid-sentence the circle of visitors around his sickbed becomes the company at his death.

translation: They lament a dead man and raise a cry
that keeps awake every weeper, every listener who rejoices.
49.sharh: Al-Mu'aybid understands the last listener as someone glad of the death. The word can also suggest a companion in weeping, which would bring the ending back to the consolation missing at the deserted camp.

1.1.5-6.head: أُمّ مَعبَد
1.1.5-6.meaning: Umm Ma'bad, the woman identified here by her kin name whose home he recognises.

1.2.5.head: تَجَلُّد
1.2.5.meaning: Making an effort to appear steadfast.

2.2.4-5.head: صَرَّدَ
2.2.4-5.meaning: No stinting in the pouring. To dispense a drink this way was to give less than would satisfy thirst.

3.2.2-3.head: جَيب السِّربال
3.2.2-3.meaning: The neck opening of his shirt, where the tears have run.

3.2.6.head: مُسعِد
3.2.6.meaning: Someone who weeps alongside the mourner and gives comfort.

4.2.7.head: قَصَدَ
4.2.7.meaning: Keep within bounds when reproaching someone.

5.1.6.head: كُنه
5.1.6.meaning: Its true object or proper place.

5.2.2.meaning: A doubling or doing something over again, here a renewed rebuke.

7.1.5.head: ذِلَّة
7.1.5.meaning: Abasement. The Jamhara has ladhdha, a pleasure, which gives folly a different attraction.

9.2.1.head: كِفاح
9.2.1.meaning: Face to face, without a barrier.

10.2.3.head: حِجل
10.2.3.meaning: Two rings about the ankles, suggesting the prisoner's restricted stride.

12.1.7.meaning: Ruin or death. The Jamhara instead speaks of wealth a person has sent ahead in life.

13.1.1.head: حُمَّ
13.1.1.meaning: Was decreed for an appointed time.

13.2.3.head: وُسِّدَ
13.2.3.meaning: Was given something on which to rest the head.

15.2.6.head: مُفَنِّد
15.2.6.meaning: A faultfinder who accuses another of poor judgement.

16.2.1.head: راحَ
16.2.1.meaning: Come in the evening, paired with coming in the morning.

17.1.1-2.head: بُليَ وأَبلى
17.1.1-2.meaning: I underwent trials and in turn tested other people.

18.1.3.head: بِدع
18.1.3.meaning: The first or unprecedented instance of something.

18.2.6.head: أَسعُد
18.2.6.meaning: Turns of good fortune succeeding adversity.

19.1.5.head: الخَنا
19.1.5.meaning: Obscenity or indecency, especially in speech.

20.2.4.head: مُطالِب
20.2.4.meaning: The benefactor who now has a claim on your gratitude.

21.2.2.head: نَكى
21.2.2.meaning: Inflict a hurt that the enemy feels.

22.1.7.head: هَوادَة
22.1.7.meaning: Leniency or forbearance when in a position of power.

22.2.5-6.head: حِفظ مَشهَد
22.2.5-6.meaning: Standing by someone in a dangerous situation. Another reading speaks of warding off that danger.

23.1.6.head: لاعَ
23.1.6.meaning: Grow upset or impatient with the reply to your teasing.

23.2.5.head: تَزَنَّدَ
23.2.5.meaning: Lose your temper at a reply. Another reading warns against going too far in what you say.

24.2.5.head: أُنكِدَ
24.2.5.meaning: Be denied a gift or get little for your trouble.

28.2.3.head: طارِف
28.2.3.meaning: Newly acquired. A term for property used here of honour.

29.2.1.head: شَعَبَ
29.2.1.meaning: Will separate him, echoing the following name of death.

29.2.3.head: شَعوب
29.2.3.meaning: A name for death understood as the separator.

31.1.1-3.head: عَدّى القَول
31.1.1-3.meaning: Direct your speech away from him to another, in Ibn Qutayba's explanation.

31.2.6.head: صَرَمَ
31.2.6.meaning: Break off the friendship or connection.

32.2.3.head: مُقارِن
32.2.3.meaning: The person whose close company shapes one's habits.

34.1.5.head: مَضاضَة
34.1.5.meaning: The smart of a wound. Al-Tabrizi comments on the line under Tarafa and records the attribution to Adi.

34.2.5-6.head: الحُسام المُهَنَّد
34.2.5-6.meaning: A keen-edged sword described as Indian.

36.2.4.head: رَدِيَ
36.2.4.meaning: Come to ruin, echoing the word for the worst companion.

40.2.1.head: ضَنين
40.2.1.meaning: Clinging tightly to what one possesses.

41.1.1-2.head: البَخلَة الأولى
41.1.1-2.meaning: The single initial act of withholding. Lexicographers cite this verse for the word's sense.

41.2.5.head: لُهِدَ
41.2.5.meaning: Be put down or roughly treated. Several lexical witnesses have “be held cheap.”

42.2.1.head: أَرَّخَ
42.2.1.meaning: I recorded what the days taught me. A variant has “made binding.” The sentence is compressed.

43.2.1.head: قارِعَة
43.2.1.meaning: Calamities imagined as striking the sufferer.

44.1.4.head: خَليقَة
44.1.4.meaning: A person's habitual disposition or trait.

44.2.5.head: مِجلَد
44.2.5.meaning: A cloth used to beat with in mourning. The image's function here is uncertain. A different version speaks of an aim or destination.

46.1.6.head: زاجِر
46.1.6.meaning: A deterrent. The middle consonant can sound like a second z in this recitation. Both written versions use j, as in the verb for restraining someone.

47.1.5.head: مَغَبَّة
47.1.5.meaning: The eventual outcome of a course of action.

48.2.3.head: نادِبَة
48.2.3.meaning: Women who lament a death and recall the dead person's qualities.

49.1.5.head: رَنَّة
49.1.5.meaning: A sustained, carrying cry of lament.

49.2.5.head: مُسعِد
49.2.5.meaning: The editor glosses this as someone glad of the death. The word also denotes a fellow mourner.
